name: Salzburg (Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg)
administrative_context: The Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg was a major ecclesiastical territory of the Holy Roman Empire governed by the Archbishop of Salzburg with combined spiritual and temporal authority. In 1675-1690 the prosecution focused on vagrant and beggar groups rather than settled community members, making the Salzburg case distinctive in its social targeting.
witchcraft_trials_significance: The Salzburg witch trials of 1675-1690, known as the Zauberer-Jackl (Jack the Sorcerer) trials, were unusual in targeting primarily vagrant, beggar, and travelling groups rather than settled community members. The initial accused, a young vagrant known as 'Zauberer-Jackl,' was said to have recruited a gang of young beggar-children into a sect of witches and devil-worshippers. The trials resulted in approximately 130-140 executions, disproportionately of young men and boys from vagrant communities—a significant departure from the typical female/settled community victim profile.

key_magistrates.name: Archbishop Max Gandolph von Kuenburg
key_magistrates.contribution_to_trials: Authorized and sustained the prosecution; the trials occurred under his ecclesiastical and secular authority

persecution_timeline.1675: Initial accusations; 'Zauberer-Jackl' (Paul Göldi or similar figure) identified as leader of a sect of vagrant witch-children
persecution_timeline.1677_1680: Peak prosecutions; vagrant and beggar youth executed
persecution_timeline.1680_1690: Continued prosecution; later phases target associated groups

affected_population.geographic_extent: Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg and surrounding territories
affected_population.social_reach: Unusually narrow: concentrated among vagrant, beggar, and travelling communities; settled community members less affected than in most witch panics
affected_population.gender_distribution: Unusually male-dominated compared to typical persecutions; young men and boys disproportionately represented among victims
affected_population.mortality_impact: Approximately 130-140 executed; some estimates suggest higher numbers including those who died in custody

scholarly_analysis.clark_perspective: Clark situates the Salzburg trials within the broader demonological tradition while noting their unusual social targeting: the application of the diabolical sect model to vagrant groups reflects anxieties about social order and wandering poor that were distinct from the typical community-dispute model of prosecution.
scholarly_analysis.hutton_perspective: Hutton emphasizes the Salzburg trials' departures from the typical social pattern as evidence that witch prosecution was a flexible tool that could be directed against different marginal social groups depending on local anxieties and the preoccupations of prosecuting authorities.
scholarly_analysis.ginzburg_perspective: The Salzburg testimonies about Zauberer-Jackl's youth sect, with its inversion of Christian norms and nocturnal meetings, have structural similarities to the sabbath narratives found elsewhere—suggesting the standardized confessional template was applied even to this atypical social group.

legacy_and_historiographical_importance: The Salzburg trials are analyzed by Wolfgang Behringer and in Lyndal Roper's Witch Craze, where the unusual social targeting is discussed. The high proportion of male and youth victims distinguishes Salzburg from most European persecution sites.
primary_sources: Salzburg archiepiscopal court records; analyzed in Behringer and Roper
source_method: Published scholarship (Behringer, Roper, Levack), archiepiscopal court records
